strengths: The paper addresses an important evaluation problem: incomplete annotations and temporally ambiguous actions can penalize valid HOI predictions. Curating multiple-answer questions is a useful approach to evaluating selected interactions without requiring exhaustive scene annotation.

The 1,274-image benchmark emphasizes challenging person-specific reasoning. Multi-person scenes with different interactions increase from 7.5% in HICO-DET to 38.9%, and the three settings distinguish image-level recognition, target-person recognition, and recognition with person detection.

The experiments cover five specialized HOI methods and seven VLM configurations. Under the proposed protocol, Qwen2.5-VL-32B achieves substantial gains, including 63.16 Macro-F1 versus the strongest specialized result of 46.51 in Setting 1.

The detection analysis is informative: Qwen2.5-VL-32B falls from 69.52 to 52.94 Instance-F1 when predicted person boxes replace ground-truth boxes. The external-detector experiment and qualitative examples provide additional evidence that localization and person attribution remain important limitations.
weaknesses: The central comparison depends on an insufficiently validated adaptation of specialized detectors. Section 3.1 retains their top-five predictions and intersects these with the four choices, whereas VLMs directly condition on those choices. Valid predictions outside the choices can consume the detector's prediction budget. The ImageNet top-five analogy does not justify this decision for multi-label HOI evaluation, and no sensitivity analysis or calibrated candidate-score baseline establishes that the reported ranking is robust.

Annotation reliability is not adequately established for a benchmark whose main contribution is correcting annotation problems. Section 2.2 reports manual checks of every question, but provides no annotator counts, agreement measurements, adjudication procedure, or independent error audit. Cross-checking Qwen-rejected negatives with GPT-4o does not establish independence from Qwen2.5-VL-32B, which participates in construction and is the strongest evaluated model. The residual ambiguity and possible selection bias remain unquantified.

The evidence supports constrained HOI recognition more directly than general HOI detection superiority. Setting 3 matches detected people to a specified ground-truth target and explicitly excludes object localization; it therefore does not evaluate complete human-object detection and pairing. Figure 1 also changes the dataset, task, and metric simultaneously, so its ranking reversal cannot isolate the effect of incomplete annotations. The claims of new state-of-the-art HOI detection performance exceed what this protocol establishes.

Several essential benchmark details are missing: the redistribution algorithm, final class coverage and per-class support, positive-answer cardinality distribution, treatment of unsupported classes in Macro-F1, and handling of unmatched or multiple matching detections. Appendix D supplies useful prompts but omits fine-tuning hyperparameters and precise reproduced-checkpoint configurations. These omissions limit reproducibility and interpretation, especially when some rare classes have only a few examples.

Some interpretations overstate the numerical evidence. The claimed clear decline from Setting 1 to Setting 2 is not general: Qwen2.5-VL-32B improves from 67.19 to 69.52 Instance-F1, and InternVL3-38B improves from 63.17 to 67.41. Precision decreases and qualitative examples support attribution difficulties, but the reported 20–25% error attribution lacks an explained audit protocol. Overall, the benchmark has worthwhile diagnostic value, but unresolved comparison fairness and annotation validation concerns currently outweigh the case for acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful evaluation problem: incomplete HOI annotations and temporal ambiguity can penalize plausible predictions. Multiple-answer questions with curated negatives offer a useful complementary assessment of interaction understanding.

The benchmark includes 1,274 images, manual checking of every question, and substantially more multi-person scenes with different interactions than HICO-DET (38.9% versus 7.5%). These choices target relevant challenges in assigning actions to individuals.

The experiments cover seven VLM configurations and five specialized HOI methods. Qwen2.5-VL-32B achieves substantial reported Macro-F1 gains, including 63.16% versus the strongest specialized result of 46.51% in Setting 1.

The detection bottleneck is supported by complementary evidence: Qwen2.5-VL-32B's Instance-F1 falls from 69.52% with ground-truth person boxes to 52.94% with its own detections, then reaches 67.29% with DETR. Appendix D also provides useful prompts and qualitative failure examples.
weaknesses: The central comparison is insufficiently controlled. VLMs directly receive four candidate answers, whereas specialized methods have their unrestricted predictions truncated to the top five before matching choices (Section 3.1). This can discard valid candidate interactions because unrelated predictions rank higher. The ImageNet top-5 analogy does not justify this multi-label decision rule, and no sensitivity analysis or candidate-conditioned scoring baseline establishes that the reported ranking is robust. This materially weakens the claim of a fair comparison.

The conclusions extend beyond the evaluated task. Setting 3 checks detection of a specified person and recognition among supplied choices; it explicitly excludes object localization and does not evaluate complete human-object detection triplets. This is a useful human-centric recognition benchmark, but it does not establish new state-of-the-art HOI detection generally. Figure 1 also compares mAP and F1 on different evaluation setups, which cannot isolate the effect of incomplete annotations.

Annotation reliability and independence are not sufficiently established for a benchmark contribution. Manual checking and GPT-4o cross-checking are positive steps, but the manuscript gives no annotator counts, agreement measurements, adjudication protocol, or measured residual false-negative rate. Qwen2.5-VL-32B participates in filtering and is subsequently evaluated; cross-checking its rejected negatives does not demonstrate the absence of selection bias. The treatment of positives also needs clarification: they are initially described as inherited ground truth, but manual refinement adds temporally plausible alternatives without quantifying or validating those additions.

Several simultaneous changes—answer choices, annotation refinement, hard-case selection, class redistribution, and evaluation metrics—are not disentangled. Increasing train-test KL divergence does not itself establish a more valid evaluation or demonstrate reliance on spurious priors. Without controlled comparisons, it remains unclear which changes produce the ranking reversal. Answer-count statistics, simple select-all or prior-based baselines, class coverage, and uncertainty estimates are particularly relevant for interpreting F1 on this small, deliberately redistributed test set.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the supplied inference prompts. The manuscript does not adequately specify the redistribution algorithm, annotation/filtering prompts, fine-tuning hyperparameters, or handling of unmatched and duplicate person detections. A separate presentation issue is that the claimed downward performance trend from Setting 1 to Setting 2 is not general: Qwen2.5-VL-32B improves in Instance-F1, Micro-F1, and exact match. Overall, the benchmark concept and diagnostic findings have merit, but unresolved comparison fairness and annotation-validation concerns currently outweigh the evidence for acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful evaluation problem: incomplete HOI annotations and temporally ambiguous actions can penalize visually plausible predictions. Curated multiple-answer questions offer a useful complementary way to assess interaction understanding.

The three settings separate image-level recognition, recognition for a specified person, and recognition requiring person detection. The 1,274-image benchmark emphasizes challenging scenes, increasing the proportion of multi-person images with different interactions from 7.5% to 38.9%.

The evaluation includes seven VLM configurations and five specialized HOI methods, with complementary class-level and instance-level metrics. Qwen2.5-VL-32B achieves substantial reported gains, including 63.16 Macro-F1 versus the strongest specialized result of 46.51 in Setting 1.

The localization bottleneck is supported by a useful intervention: replacing VLM detection with DETR increases Qwen2.5-VL-32B's Setting 3 Instance-F1 from 52.94 to 67.29. The person-attribution error analysis and qualitative examples also identify practically relevant failure modes.
weaknesses: The central cross-family comparison is insufficiently controlled. Section 3.1 converts specialized detectors into answers by retaining their top five predictions and intersecting them with the four choices, whereas VLMs receive the choices before answering. Relevant choices can therefore be excluded by unrelated high-ranking detector outputs. The ImageNet top-5 analogy does not justify this multi-label decision rule. There is no sensitivity analysis over k or comparison with candidate-restricted scores and validation-calibrated thresholds, so the reported ranking may partly reflect the adapter rather than interaction understanding.

Annotation validity is essential to the contribution but remains inadequately established. Although every question receives manual checking, the paper does not report annotator counts, agreement, adjudication procedures, or an independent audit of residual false negatives. Figure 4 raises a concrete concern: the apple example accepts only 'peel apple' while offering 'hold apple' as an incorrect choice, despite the visible hand holding the apple. Moreover, cross-checking Qwen-rejected negatives with another VLM does not establish that using an evaluated model during construction introduces no selection bias.

The claim that large VLMs establish new state-of-the-art HOI detection performance exceeds what this protocol measures. Object localization is explicitly excluded, candidate interactions are supplied, and Setting 3 evaluates the detected person overlapping a known target rather than exhaustive human-object triplet detection. These are useful tasks, but they do not establish superiority on conventional HOI detection. Figure 1 additionally changes the dataset, metric, candidate space, and localization requirements simultaneously, so it cannot attribute the performance reversal specifically to annotation shortcomings.

Several conclusions are stronger than the reported evidence. The claimed downward performance trend from Setting 1 to Setting 2 is not general: Qwen2.5-VL-32B's Instance-F1 increases from 67.19 to 69.52 and its EM from 23.16 to 35.01. Lower precision supports a narrower interpretation, while the attribution-error percentages lack a described sampling and categorization procedure. Similarly, increased train-test KL divergence establishes distribution shift, not that the original evaluation measured reliance on priors.

Important reproducibility details are missing, including class coverage and per-class support after redistribution, the redistribution algorithm, handling of unmatched or duplicate person detections, and fine-tuning hyperparameters. These omissions matter particularly for Macro-F1 on a small, deliberately redistributed dataset. Overall, the useful benchmark concept and diagnostic findings are outweighed by unresolved comparison fairness and annotation reliability concerns that directly affect the paper's main conclusions.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful evaluation problem: incomplete HOI annotations can penalize visually valid predictions. The 200-image audit in Appendix A.1 provides concrete evidence, including missing person/object annotations in 29% of images and incomplete action labels in 24.5%.

The benchmark represents substantial curation effort: 3,773 questions across three source datasets, with emphasis on multi-person scenes and fine-grained interactions. Four annotators reviewed the main benchmark, modifying 38.39% of choices, with reported pairwise agreement of 95.22%.

The experimental coverage is substantial. It includes five specialized methods, several VLM families and sizes, detector-assisted evaluation, human–object localization variants, fine-tuning, prediction-selection ablations, bootstrap intervals, and an ablation excluding Qwen from screening.

The separation of localization and recognition provides useful diagnostic evidence. For example, Qwen2.5-VL-32B improves from 52.94 to 69.52 Instance-F1 when supplied with person boxes. The reported cross-person attribution errors also identify a practically relevant challenge.
weaknesses: The central claim of a fair cross-paradigm comparison remains insufficiently established. VLMs explicitly condition on four candidate answers, while specialized models select their top five predictions from the full vocabulary before intersecting with those candidates. This can discard a correct candidate because unrelated classes rank higher. The ablations do not resolve this asymmetry: Table 11 shows that top-10 raises ADA-CM Instance-F1 from 47.74 to 50.58 and Micro-F1 from 61.68 to 63.50, substantially narrowing the headline VLM advantage. Candidate-restricted scoring and independently calibrated selection rules are missing.

There is a consequential unresolved scoring inconsistency. Table 1 reports Qwen3-VL Macro-F1 of 29.10 despite Instance-F1 of 0.25, Micro-F1 of 0.51, and recall of 0.26. Near-zero recall explains high precision over a tiny predicted set, but does not explain this Macro-F1 under Appendix C's fixed-class averaging formula and the stated 600-class coverage. The treatment of undetected targets, empty predictions, and zero-support classes needs explicit reconciliation. Some repeated results also disagree, such as ADA-CM Macro-F1 in Tables 1 and 11. These issues affect confidence in the benchmark's scoring, rather than merely presentation.

The main conclusions overstate evidence for full HOI detection. Default Setting 1 requires person localization but does not verify the interacted object's box; candidate labels also constrain the recognition problem. In the actual human–object detection variant, Table 13 reports only 11.48 Instance-F1 for standalone Qwen2.5-VL-32B versus 42.10 for ADA-CM. The appendix appropriately describes MCQA as diagnostic, but the main framing should consistently distinguish candidate-conditioned interaction recognition from full HOI detection. Comparing F1 on this changed task against original HICO-DET mAP does not isolate the effect of annotation incompleteness.

The annotation policy conflates simultaneous actions with mutually exclusive but visually plausible alternatives. Treating both boarding and exiting as required positives means that predicting one defensible interpretation loses recall. Consequently, measured 'incomplete multi-action recognition' can reflect failure to enumerate uncertainty rather than failure to recognize concurrent actions. Reported annotator agreement is valuable, but does not resolve this construct-validity issue; ambiguous alternatives and genuine co-occurring actions need separate analysis.

Several diagnostic conclusions exceed their controls. Uniform answer positions do not rule out language-only or option-co-occurrence shortcuts, and no text-only baseline is reported. The 200-case failure analysis deliberately selects cases where ADA-CM succeeds and the VLM fails, so its percentages cannot establish comparative error prevalence generally. Likewise, cross-dataset comparisons involving different label spaces require explicit accounting for which labels each specialized model can predict. Overall, the curated resource has worthwhile potential, but unresolved scoring validity and comparison fairness currently outweigh the evidence supporting acceptance.

strengths: The benchmark addresses a meaningful evaluation problem. The 200-image HICO-DET audit identifies missing person/object annotations in 29% of images and incomplete action labels in 24.5%, providing concrete motivation for evaluating explicitly verified candidate interactions.

Dataset construction involves substantial human verification: 3,773 questions across three source datasets, four annotators, and reported pairwise agreement of 95.22%. Manual refinement changes 38.39% of the main benchmark’s options, extending the contribution beyond automated question generation.

The experimental coverage is substantial: multiple VLM families, five specialized methods, detector-assisted evaluation, human–object localization variants, fine-tuning, bootstrap intervals, and prediction-selection ablations. Table 12 also directly investigates the potential bias from using Qwen during construction.

The separation of recognition and localization provides useful diagnostic evidence. For example, Qwen2.5-VL-32B improves from 52.94 to 69.52 Instance-F1 when target boxes are supplied. The benchmark could be useful for studying grounding and interaction attribution even without establishing general superiority over specialized detectors.
weaknesses: The central comparison gives the paradigms different candidate-selection problems. VLMs receive four options before predicting, whereas specialized methods first select their top five predictions from the full vocabulary and only then intersect with the options. Correct candidate scores can therefore be discarded because unrelated classes rank higher. The appendix’s threshold and top-K experiments acknowledge sensitivity but do not resolve this asymmetry. Indeed, Table 11 increases ADA-CM Instance-F1 from 47.74 to 50.58 with top-10, substantially narrowing the headline advantage over specialized models. Candidate-restricted scoring with independently calibrated selection is needed to substantiate a fair cross-paradigm comparison.

A consequential metric inconsistency remains unexplained. Table 1 reports Qwen3-VL Macro-F1 of 29.10% alongside Instance-F1 of 0.25% and Micro-F1 of 0.51%. Under Appendix C’s formulas, 1,274 four-option questions and 0.25% Instance-F1 permit only approximately 13 true-positive option selections; averaging class F1 over the claimed 600-class coverage could not then yield 29.10%. Near-zero detection recall explains high precision, as the authors discuss, but not this Macro-F1 result. The evaluated class set, treatment of missed detections, and implementation must be reconciled before the rankings are reliable.

The headline framing overstates what the default task establishes about HOI detection. Setting 1 checks human localization while leaving object localization implicit. In the actual human–object detection variant, Table 13 reports only 11.48 Instance-F1 for standalone Qwen2.5-VL-32B versus 42.10 for ADA-CM. The appendix acknowledges this limitation, but it materially qualifies the abstract’s cross-paradigm conclusions. Similarly, comparing HICO-DET mAP with the new benchmark’s F1 in Figure 1 cannot isolate the effect of annotation correction because the task, candidate space, dataset composition, and metric all change.

The annotation policy conflates simultaneous interactions with alternative interpretations. Both boarding and exiting can be required positives when a static image cannot distinguish them. Set-based recall then penalizes selecting only one plausible interpretation, just as it penalizes missing a genuinely concurrent action such as holding an object. Consequently, the reported multi-action weakness partly measures exhaustive enumeration of uncertainty. High annotator agreement does not resolve this construct-validity issue; these two kinds of positives need separate analysis.

Some supporting interpretations exceed the controls provided. The detailed 200-case failure analysis selects cases where ADA-CM succeeds and Qwen fails, so it cannot establish their relative overall prevalence of those errors. Uniform answer positions do not rule out semantic or language-only shortcuts, and increased train–test KL divergence does not itself demonstrate more reliable evaluation. These concerns are secondary to the comparison and metric issues, but collectively limit the stronger claims. Despite the resource’s worthwhile merits and extensive experiments, the unresolved validity of its central comparison favors weak rejection.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful evaluation problem: incomplete HOI annotations can penalize visually valid predictions. The 200-image audit in Appendix A.1 provides concrete supporting evidence, and explicit positive and negative choices offer a useful diagnostic alternative.

Dataset curation involves substantial human effort. The benchmark contains 3,773 questions across three source datasets; four annotators revised 38.39% of the main benchmark’s choices, with reported 95.22% pairwise agreement. This supports the resource’s potential usefulness beyond simply repackaging existing annotations.

The experimental coverage is substantial: multiple VLM families, five specialized methods, localization-controlled evaluations, detector-assisted variants, human–object-pair evaluation, and fine-tuning experiments. The appendix also includes confidence intervals and an ablation excluding Qwen from screening.

The localization bottleneck is convincingly demonstrated. Qwen2.5-VL-32B achieves 52.94 Instance-F1 with standalone person detection, 67.29 with an external detector, and 69.52 with ground-truth boxes. These diagnostic findings remain useful independently of claims about which paradigm performs best.
weaknesses: A material scoring inconsistency needs resolution. Table 1 reports Qwen3-VL at 29.10% Macro-F1 despite only 0.25% Instance-F1, 0.51% Micro-F1, and 100% precision. With four choices per question and the stated fixed 600-class evaluation, near-zero true-positive counts cannot support such a large macro average under Appendix C’s formula. The explanation about detection failures addresses precision but not Macro-F1. Whether missed classes or questions are excluded is crucial to trusting the benchmark rankings.

The cross-paradigm comparison is sensitive to prediction conversion. VLMs see the four candidate answers, whereas specialized detectors have their unrestricted predictions truncated before matching candidates. Table 11 shows that increasing ADA-CM from top-5 to top-10 improves all three F1 metrics, reaching 50.58 Instance-F1 and substantially narrowing the headline gap to Qwen’s 52.94. The claim that top-5 provides the best precision–recall balance is therefore not supported by those F1 results. Candidate-restricted scoring and validation-based calibration would better establish comparison fairness.

The main paper overstates what is established about full HOI detection. Default Setting 1 requires person localization but infers objects through interaction labels. When both human and object localization are required, Table 13 reports only 11.48 Instance-F1 for standalone Qwen2.5-VL-32B versus 42.10 for ADA-CM. The appendix acknowledges this distinction, but the abstract and main narrative should scope VLM competitiveness to the evaluated person-centered task.

Some conclusions extend beyond the controls. Position randomization does not establish the absence of language-only shortcuts, and negative agreement does not establish unbiased benchmark selection, although the screening ablation is helpful. Likewise, the 200-case analysis explicitly selects VLM failures where ADA-CM succeeds; it identifies failure types but cannot independently establish their relative prevalence across paradigms.

Reproducibility is helped by prompts and annotation details, but the scoring inconsistencies and model-specific coordinate handling remain consequential. In particular, querying InternVL for its perceived image dimensions does not verify coordinate alignment, which matters when localization drives the findings. Overall, the curated resource and diagnostic breadth place this near the acceptance boundary, but unresolved scoring validity and comparison fairness prevent a confident acceptance recommendation.
